passage: Divyansh was new in the colony, and Binita was walking him home from school. “Which way to your house?” he asked. Binita couldn't find the words, so she traced the road in the air with one finger: a long straight line, then a little hook, then a wide curve. “Ah, the hook is the sweet shop!” said Divyansh. “And the curve goes round the park.” Binita nodded, surprised. “Yes! Turn right at the sweet shop, and left after the park.” The words came easily after the gesture, as if her hand had found them first.

qa.q: What did Binita trace in the air?
qa.a: She traced the road in the air with one finger.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she could not find the words, and what did her gesture do?
qa.a: She was probably a bit stuck and unsure how to explain. Tracing the road helped her sort out the route, and the words came easily after.

qa.q: What could an adult do to help a child explaining a route?
qa.a: Let the child gesture and ask what the hook or curve stands for, so the gesture can help the child think.

qa.q: How might Divyansh find Binita's gesture compared with words?
qa.a: Easier to follow, since he could work out the sweet shop and the park from the shapes. He was new and probably glad to get a clear picture.

grounding: A child traces a map in the air to explain the way home; gesture helps thought and explanation.

passage:
“Dhruv, how did the ball end up in Mrs Pai's garden?” asked Manoj, his father.
“It went like this.” Dhruv drew a circle in the air with his finger. “It hit the shed wall and came back and then, whoosh, up.”
“Show me again slowly.”
Dhruv traced it once more, frowning. “Oh! It hit the shed roof first. That's why it went the wrong way.”
“So it bounced off the roof.”
“Yes!”
Manoj smiled and let him keep moving his hands. “I'll go and say sorry to Mrs Pai. Want to come?”

qa.q: Whose garden did the ball end up in?
qa.a: It ended up in Mrs Pai's garden.

qa.q: What was Dhruv thinking when he traced the ball's path a second time?
qa.a: He was working out what really happened, and the tracing helped him realise the ball hit the shed roof first. He was probably a little worried about the trouble.

qa.q: What did Manoj do that helped Dhruv explain?
qa.a: He asked him to show it again slowly and let him keep moving his hands, so Dhruv could work out the route himself.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pai feel about the ball, and what would Manoj's visit change?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised or annoyed by the ball in her garden, and an apology would show that the family cares. She may also just be glad to know what happened.

grounding: A child traces a ball's path in the air to explain it, and gesturing helps the child work out the idea.

passage: I'm Mehak. When Gargi, the new girl, asked how to get to my house for the project, words just weren't working. “Past the temple, then… no, before the temple…” So I drew it in the air with my finger: a straight line for the main road, a loop round the park, a sharp left at the chemist. Halfway through, my finger stopped. “Wait. If you cut through the park here,” I jabbed at the air, “you skip the whole loop.” I'd never noticed that, even though I walk it every day. Gargi copied the shape in the air with her own finger and nodded. She got there in ten minutes.

qa.q: Where is the sharp left in Mehak's directions?
qa.a: The sharp left is at the chemist.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when the finger stopped halfway?
qa.a: Mehak felt surprised and pleased at discovering a shortcut through the park while tracing the route.

qa.q: Why did tracing in the air work better than words?
qa.a: It let Mehak show the shape of the route and think it through, finding a shortcut that words had missed.

qa.q: How might Gargi, new to the area, have found the air map?
qa.a: Gargi could copy the shape with her own finger, which made the route easier to picture and remember.

grounding: Shows a child tracing a map in the air to explain the way home, and the gesture helping the child work out a new idea.

passage: Class note, Monday. Devika, science. In today's oral quiz I asked Bidisha how a thrown ball moves. She started, “It goes up and then…” and stopped, hands clamped under her desk. Last term another teacher told her to keep her hands still when answering. I said, “Use your hands if it helps.” Her finger shot up and drew a smooth arch in the air: rising, slowing at the top, then curving down faster. “Up slow, then down fast. Like a rainbow, but lopsided because of the wind.” That was a better answer than most of my older classes give. Note to self: let children gesture while they explain.

qa.q: What shape did Bidisha draw in the air?
qa.a: Bidisha drew a smooth arch in the air.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha stop and clamp her hands under her desk?
qa.a: She was probably anxious about being told off, since another teacher had told her to keep her hands still, and without them she felt stuck.

qa.q: What did Devika do that helped Bidisha explain?
qa.a: Devika told her to use her hands if it helped, which let Bidisha show and work out the ball's path.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had kept the no-hands rule?
qa.a: Bidisha might have stayed stuck, and Devika would never have heard how well she understood the ball's path.

grounding: Shows a child tracing a ball's route in the air to explain it, and how letting children gesture aids explanation.

passage: Wednesday. Aadhya's diary. Today at break Payal didn't get how I'd scored in the carrom game yesterday. I tried saying it: “The striker hit the side, then came back and knocked the red in.” She looked blank. So I traced it in the air, again and again: my finger shot to the edge, bounced off at an angle and zigzagged back to the corner. While I was drawing it, I suddenly understood why it worked: the angle in was the same as the angle out! Payal copied the zigzag with her finger and said, “Oh! Like a ball off a wall.” Tomorrow I'm going to try it on purpose.

qa.q: What did Aadhya's striker knock in?
qa.a: The striker knocked the red in.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling while tracing the shot?
qa.a: Aadhya felt excited and surprised, suddenly understanding that the angle in matched the angle out.

qa.q: Why is it worth letting children gesture when explaining?
qa.a: Tracing helped Aadhya explain the shot to Payal and also work out the idea, which words alone had not done.

qa.q: How did Payal understand the shot in the end?
qa.a: Payal copied the zigzag with her own finger and linked it to a ball bouncing off a wall.

grounding: Shows a child tracing a path in the air to explain a shot, and the gesture helping the child work out the idea.

passage:
Indu Didi had just started teaching at the new tuition centre in Kasaragod and had no idea where anything was. "Ishita, how do I get to your house for Sunday lunch?"

Ishita frowned. "You go… um…" Her words stuck. So her finger took over, drawing in the air: a long straight line past the temple, a big loop round the pond, then a sharp hook. "Left at the banyan tree! I forgot that till my hand did it."

Indu Didi traced the same path with her own finger, slowly, while Ishita watched. "Straight, round the pond, left at the banyan."

"Yes! And our gate is the blue one."

qa.q: What colour is Ishita's gate?
qa.a: The blue one.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when her finger found the turn she had forgotten?
qa.a: Relieved and pleased 😊, as "Left at the banyan tree!" shows, after feeling stuck when the words wouldn't come.

qa.q: What did Indu Didi do that helped Ishita explain?
qa.a: She let Ishita gesture without hurrying her, then traced the same path back to check she had understood.

qa.q: What would change if Indu Didi had said, "Just tell me, don't wave your hands"?
qa.a: Ishita might have stayed stuck, since her hand was helping her remember the route, and Indu Didi would get worse directions.

grounding: It shows a child tracing a route in the air to give directions, the gesture helping her remember the turn, and an adult letting her gesture.
